description: Sol Survivors is an interactive 3D educational survival game where children aged 7–12 experience life as astronauts on Mars. Players manage a Martian outpost, balancing essential resources like oxygen, water, food, and electricity. They operate facilities, grow crops, maintain life-support systems, and protect their base from dust storms and solar radiation. Inspired by NASA missions, the game makes learning about space exploration and resource management fun, engaging, and hands-on.
summary:
Sol Survivors is a first-person 3D survival game that trains junior astronauts aged 7 to 12 to run the first human base on Mars. Your crew lands in five sols (Mars days); until then you keep the base alive alone. Each morning you read the forecast and share limited solar energy between the ice melter, the greenhouse and two shields. You melt ice for water, grow food, fix leaks, clean dusty solar panels and survive solar storms.

It addresses the challenge by turning real NASA data into each day's rules. The sols are real Martian days measured by NASA's InSight lander: the real night cold (down to -97 °C) raises the ice melter's energy need, and the real wind cuts your solar power. The solar storms are real coronal mass ejections from May 2024 in NASA's DONKI database, timed by NASA's predicted arrival at Mars. A NASA DATA screen shows every number and its source, a Mars Trek map and real mission photos.

It is important because it lets children learn by doing. A child who finishes knows how cold Mars is, how thin its air is and why a solar storm is dangerous, because they survived the real ones.
details:
What it does

Sol Survivors is a first-person 3D game for Windows PC, built in Unity for children aged 7 to 12. You are the only person on the first human base on Mars, and your crew lands in five sols. Each sol lasts about three minutes. If food, water or a shield runs out, only that sol restarts, so losing teaches without punishing.

How it works

  • Seven bars to manage: food, water, energy, ice melter, greenhouse, radiation shield and storm shield.
  • The morning forecast is the puzzle. It shows the real weather, how much solar energy you will collect and how much each machine needs. You collect energy at the power hub, share it between four machines, and keep some back for later.
  • Water: the ice melter fills the tank while it has power; you drink at the tank.
  • Food: twelve grow beds with three kinds of crop. They grow only while the greenhouse has power and the tank has water. You harvest ripe beds and replant them.
  • Each sol adds one new problem. Sol 1 is a guided tutorial with a tour of every room. Sol 2 has a leaking pipe to repair with a tool kit. On Sol 3 you put on a spacesuit, go out through the airlock and brush dust off the solar panels. Sols 3, 4 and 5 have solar storms.
  • Solar storm event: a countdown runs to the storm's arrival, alarms sound at 30 and 10 seconds, then the storm hits and the radiation shield drains several times faster. You must save energy for it.
  • Surprise jobs during a sol: a clogged water recycler and a shield that drifts out of tune. Each one comes with a short "did you know?" fact.
  • Herbie, the helper robot, gives new Mars facts every sol.
  • Four mission fragments are hidden outside. Each shows a real NASA photo and the story of a real mission: Viking 1, Sojourner, Opportunity, and Perseverance with Ingenuity. Finding all four gives bonus energy every sol.
  • Up to three stars per sol, replay of any sol, and a final mission summary with a rank.
  • Main menu, sol picker, intro and ending stories, pause menu, and settings for graphics, frame rate, mouse sensitivity, volume and display. Progress is saved between sessions.
  • Sound: base hum, Mars wind, footsteps, alarms, Geiger clicks and calm music. Every sound is synthesised by code when the game starts; there are no audio files.
  • Picture: a butterscotch Mars sky, warm low sunlight, dust blowing from the real wind direction, a red pulse during storms, and a HUD whose bars animate and warn when low.

How NASA data drives the game

All data is stored inside the game, so it works offline.

  • NASA InSight Mars Weather Service: five real sols (InSight sols 676 to 680, 20 to 24 October 2020). The real night-time low raises the ice melter's energy need. The real top wind lowers the solar energy you collect and makes the storm shield work harder. It also sets how much dust you see and how loud the wind is outside. A live strip on the HUD shows outside temperature, wind and air pressure.
  • NASA DONKI: three real coronal mass ejections from sunspot AR 13664 in May 2024. Each storm's speed sets how hard the radiation surge is, and NASA's predicted arrival time at Mars sets when it hits in the sol. The fastest (2,225 km/s) is kept for Sol 5.
  • NASA Mars Trek: a real map of the InSight landing site in Elysium Planitia on the NASA DATA screen.
  • NASA Image and Video Library: six real mission photos, each with its credit line.
  • The NASA DATA screen in the main menu lists every real number, where it came from and what it changes in the game.

We say this plainly in the game: the weather is from 2020 and the storms are from 2024, two real records played together. The sols are ordered from the calmest wind to the windiest so the game gets harder. The size of each effect is scaled for play; DONKI gives a storm's speed and timing, not a radiation dose.

Benefits

  • For children: they learn by doing the job. Each action comes with a one-line reason: why ice is melted, why plants need power and water, why a shield matters.
  • For teachers and parents: the sols are short, the game works offline, and it needs only a keyboard and a mouse. A mistake restarts one sol, so no child gets stuck.
  • For trust: every real number is shown with its NASA source, so an adult can check what the child learned.

Intended impact

A child who finishes knows how cold a Martian night is, how thin the air is and why a solar storm is dangerous. We want real NASA data to be something a seven-year-old can feel, and we want players to leave curious about space and about the real missions whose photos they found.

Tools, coding languages, hardware and software

  • Software: Unity 6 (6000.3) with the Universal Render Pipeline, Blender for the base's 3D props, and Git for version control.
  • Coding languages: C# for the game, and Python for the script that turns the raw NASA downloads into the game's data file.
  • Hardware: made and tested on Windows PCs. It runs on a Windows 10 or 11 PC with a keyboard and mouse; no special hardware is needed.
  • AI tools: Claude by Anthropic (see "Use of SI (AI) tools" below).

How it is creative

Real data is not shown as a chart. It is the rule set of each day. A windier real sol gives you less power. A faster real storm gives you a harder surge. Every sound is generated in code, and the wind you hear is as loud as the wind InSight measured.

Factors our team considered

  • Age: short sols, large text, one new idea per sol, and a restart of only the failed sol.
  • Honesty: every real number has its source on screen, and anything scaled for play is labelled.
  • Reliability: no network connection is needed, so it works in a classroom or at a judging table.
  • Credit: NASA photo credits are shown in the game, and every outside resource is listed on this page.
